subject: Performance SLO (p95/p99) qualification - hosted API vs current provider - post-call recap

Subject: Re: Performance SLO (p95/p99) qualification - hosted API vs current provider - post-call recap

Hi Alex - thanks again for the call earlier. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we keep momentum: 

Summary of ask
- Finlytics wants end-to-end latency SLOs for your main text generation flow (inference request -> model output -> app render) at p95/p99.
- Key constraints: <20s max response for long streaming jobs, target interactive latency for short prompts (single-shot), predictable p95/p99 under your expected concurrency.

What we covered on the call
- Current provider: you see ~p95 240ms, p99 ~750ms for 1k token completion workloads under your benchmark; occasional spikes under peak concurrency.
- You'd like us to validate hosted API performance vs the current provider using a small canary run with representative traffic.

Initial next steps (proposed)
1) You share a 24-48h sample of typical traffic (anonymized requests + typical payload sizes).
2) We run a controlled canary (our hosted API) scaled to your target concurrency and return p50/p95/p99 numbers plus a CSV of raw latencies.
3) Post-run call to review results and discuss rollout options (dedicated capacity or routing policies) and any required SLAs.

I've attached our runbook and an example CSV from a recent evaluation for reference. Marissa - looping you in for the test plan and timing. Aditya - FYI on procurement and deal path.

If that looks right I can schedule the canary for next week - what days/times work for you?

Best,
Laura
Laura Bennett
Senior Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
redwoodinference.com

Attachments: redwood_perf_runbook.pdf (3 pages), p95_p99_test_results.csv (sample)

Thanks Laura - that recap is helpful. A few clarifying Qs before we hand over traffic: 

1) When you report p95/p99, does that measure end-to-end from our client (US-East) including network + your hosted ingress, or is it service-side only? We need E2E for procurement.
2) Concurrency model - we run a mix of short (50-100 tokens) and long (up to 2k tokens) completions. What concurrency should we expect per session and does your hosted API support streaming for partial token delivery?
3) Cold start behavior - if we spin up a new region/instance for a canary, do you see large cold-start spikes?

We can share an anonymized 48-hour traffic dump. Prefer Wed/Thu next week for the canary window.

Alex

Subject: Re: Performance SLO (p95/p99) qualification - hosted API vs current provider - post-call recap

Alex - great Qs, answers below. I've also sketched the exact reporting we'll provide so procurement has what it needs.

Q1) Measurement scope
- Our canary will collect end-to-end latencies from a client in the same region you operate (we can run from us-east-1 to match). The p95/p99 we report will include network RTT to our ingress, request queuing and model inference time, and initial token delivery time for streaming workloads. We'll label each measurement with request size and whether streaming was used.

Q2) Concurrency and streaming
- Concurrency model: the canary will simulate your mix (short vs long). For planning, assume we can sustain a steady 8 concurrent active requests per virtual client and burst to 32 across the canary pool without queueing if we size correctly.
- Streaming: yes - our hosted API supports streaming (chunked token delivery). For long-running completions we measure time-to-first-token and time-to-last-token; p95/p99 are reported for both.

Q3) Cold starts
- Cold start impact is small for models we serve on hosted capacity (we use pre-warmed pools), but for brand-new dedicated nodes there can be a modest warm-up (200-700ms) for the first request while kernels and KV caches initialize. We'll explicitly mark warmup-only samples in the CSV.

Reporting deliverables for procurement
- CSV with raw latencies (request_id, timestamp, request_size_tokens, time_to_first_token_ms, time_to_last_token_ms, total_e2e_ms)
- Summary: p50/p95/p99 for time_to_first_token and total_e2e for short and long buckets
- Notes on test config: region, concurrency profile, payload distribution, whether cache priming performed

If that fits, we'll plan to run Wed 2026-07-01 09:00-13:00 ET. Marissa - can you confirm test run plan and whether we need extra warmup iterations?

Thanks,
Laura

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwoodinference.com>

Subject: Re: Performance SLO (p95/p99) qualification - hosted API vs current provider - post-call recap

Hi Alex / Laura - Marissa from the infra team here. Quick technical notes and the canary run plan: 

Planned canary config (proposed)
- Region: us-east-1 (we'll run agents from the same region)
- Clients: 10 virtual clients with the following mix: 70% short (50-150 tokens), 30% long (800-2000 tokens)
- Concurrency: target 8 active requests per client (aggregate concurrency ~80), spike bursts up to 120 for 30s windows
- Streaming: enabled for long requests; time-to-first-token and full completion times captured
- Warmup: we'll do a 15min priming pass to populate KV cache and warm pools

Expected baseline numbers (hosted API, v1 profile, pre-warmed):
- Short requests (50-150 tokens): p95 ~180ms, p99 ~420ms (total e2e)
- Long requests (800-2000 tokens): p95 ~1.2s, p99 ~2.8s (time-to-last-token included)

Notes vs your reported current-provider numbers
- We typically see smaller p99s because of continuous batching + prefix caching and faster kernels; your current provider's p99 spikes at 750ms for short workloads likely reflect queuing under burst.
- If you need stricter p99 (e.g., <500ms for short), we can discuss dedicated capacity and higher pre-warm counts; that typically reduces p99 by 30-50% at cost.

I attached a CSV from a recent comparable run to give you a sense of distribution (same columns Laura listed). Happy to run the canary on Wed 2026-07-01 09:00 ET - confirm and we'll send a short pre-test checklist (IP allowlist, sample auth keys).
